chunk.text:
### Classification

| Type | Frequency | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Arterial embolism (SMA) | 40-50% | Cardiac embolus (atrial fibrillation, valvular disease, recent MI, ventricular thrombus) |
| Arterial thrombosis (SMA) | 20-30% | Atherosclerotic stenosis with acute thrombosis; history of chronic mesenteric ischemia (postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss) |
| Mesenteric venous thrombosis (MVT) | 5-15% | Hypercoagulable state, portal hypertension, intra-abdominal inflammation, malignancy |
| Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI) | 5-15% | Low-flow state (cardiogenic shock, vasopressors, dialysis, cardiac surgery) |

### Key Clinical Features

- **Pain out of proportion to physical exam** — hallmark finding; severe periumbilical or diffuse abdominal pain with minimal tenderness early
- Rapid onset (minutes to hours) with arterial embolism; more insidious with MVT (days)
- Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea (often bloody in late stage)
- History of atrial fibrillation, recent cardiac catheterization, hypercoagulability, or atherosclerotic disease
- Peritoneal signs indicate bowel necrosis — this is a late and ominous finding
- Abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds in advanced disease

### High-Risk Populations
- Atrial fibrillation (especially without anticoagulation)
- Recent MI or cardiac surgery
- Peripheral vascular disease / known aortic atherosclerosis
- Hypercoagulable states (Factor V Leiden, malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome)
- Chronic mesenteric ischemia (postprandial pain, weight loss) — at risk for acute thrombosis
- Heart failure patients on vasopressors or inotropes (NOMI)

- **Mesenteric venous thrombosis** (`acute-mesenteric-venous-thrombosis`): subacute abdominal pain, hypercoagulable state, CT with portal/mesenteric vein thrombus

### Urgent
- **Diverticulitis** (`acute-diverticulitis`): LLQ pain, low-grade fever, leukocytosis. CT for complications (abscess, perforation, fistula).
- **Pyelonephritis** (`pyelonephritis`): flank pain, fever, pyuria, CVA tenderness
- **Urolithiasis** (`urolithiasis`): colicky flank-to-groin pain, hematuria, restless patient. CT KUB without contrast.
- **Ischemic colitis** (`ischemic-colitis`): elderly, post-prandial pain, bloody diarrhea, watershed area
- **Ogilvie syndrome** (`ogilvie-syndrome`): acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, massive distension, cecal diameter > 12 cm → risk of perforation

### Non-Emergent
- **Biliary colic** (`biliary-colic`): episodic RUQ pain, post-prandial, resolves within 6 hours, no fever/leukocytosis
- **Viral gastroenteritis** (`viral-gastroenteritis`): nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, diffuse cramping, no peritoneal signs

chunk.text:
.

Abdominal compartment syndrome with very high intraabdominal pressure may cause bowel ischemia that is complicated with ischemia–reperfusion injury when decompression laparotomy is performed [35].

AMI has been described in patients with coronavirus disease (COVID -19), probably related to large vessel thromboembolic events as well as to small vessel thrombosis linked to hypercoagulability and fibrinolysis shutdown [36].Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings should be assumed to be AMI until disproven. (Strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence 1C)

The key to early diagnosis is a high level of clinical suspicion.

The clinical scenario of a patient complaining of excruciating abdominal pain with an unrevealing abdominal examination is classic for early AMI [37]. The reason for the pain being disproportionate to the clinical findings is that ischemia starts from the mucosa toward the serosa. That is why initially there is severe pain without clinical findings.

If the physical examination demonstrates signs of peritonitis, there is likely irreversible intestinal ischemia with bowel necrosis. In a study on AMI, 95% of patients presented with abdominal pain, 44% with nausea, 35% with vomiting, 35% with diarrhea, and 16% with blood per rectum [38]. Approximately, one-third of patients present with the triad of abdominal pain, fever, and hemoccult-positive stool. Other patients, particularly those with delayed diagnosis, may present in extremis with septic shock. Clinical signs of peritonitis may be subtle. Accordingly, one must have a high index of suspicion, because such findings are predictive of intestinal infarction.

chunk.text:
**Presentation:**
- Sudden onset crampy abdominal pain (typically left-sided), followed by urgency to defecate
- Mild-to-moderate bloody diarrhea or hematochezia within 24 hours of pain onset
- Classically in elderly patients (> 60 years) with cardiovascular risk factors
- Pain is out of proportion to exam findings early; progresses if ischemia worsens

**Risk factors:**
- Atherosclerosis, hypotension/shock, atrial fibrillation
- Aortic surgery (0.5-10% post-AAA repair)
- Medications: vasoconstrictors, digitalis, NSAIDs, estrogens, cocaine, methamphetamine
- Hypercoagulable states, sickle cell disease
- Long-distance running (young patients)

**Anatomic distribution:**
- Watershed areas most vulnerable: splenic flexure (Griffiths point), rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point)
- Right-sided ischemic colitis (ICA/SMA territory) — more severe, higher surgical rates, suggests acute mesenteric ischemia

**Exam findings:**
- Mild-moderate abdominal tenderness (usually left-sided)
- Hematochezia on rectal exam
- Peritoneal signs suggest transmural necrosis — emergent surgical evaluation
